   775	\subsection{Evaluation and Statistical Design}
   776	\label{sec:eval_stat_design}
   777	
   778	\subsubsection{Evaluation Metrics}
   779	\label{subsec:9pathogen_metrics}
   780	
   781	The following evaluation metrics are used in the 11-pathogen benchmark.
   782	
   783	\begin{itemize}
   784	\item \textbf{MCC (Matthews Correlation Coefficient)}: The primary evaluation metric (defined formally in Equation~\ref{eq:mcc} below).
   785	The confusion matrix is constructed using only Layer A (positive selection positions) as positive labels: TP = detected positions belonging to Layer A, FP = detected positions not belonging to Layer A, FN = undetected positions belonging to Layer A, TN = undetected positions not belonging to Layer A.
   786	Layer B (constrained regions) is not included in MCC computation and is evaluated separately via constrained FPR. The majority of genomic positions belonging to neither Layer A nor B are classified as FP or TN depending on detection status.
   787	\item \textbf{F1}: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
   788	\item \textbf{Precision}: The proportion of true positives among detected positions.
   789	\item \textbf{Recall}: The proportion of true positives detected among all true positives.
   790	\item \textbf{Enrichment ratio}: The ratio of positive density within detected regions to overall positive density.
   791	All enrichment tests used one-sided Fisher's exact test (alternative: greater), testing the directional hypothesis that hotspot positions are enriched for vaccine escape mutations relative to non-hotspot positions.
   792	\item \textbf{Constrained FPR}: The false positive rate in Layer B constrained regions.
   793	\item \textbf{DMS F1}: F1 score against Layer C DMS ground truth (computed only for 6 pathogens with DMS data).
   794	\end{itemize}
   795	
   796	Stage~1 uses the hotspot-score composite metric (defined in Eq.~\ref{eq:hotspot_score}, Section~\ref{subsec:hotspot_score}), which balances detection accuracy with reproducibility.
   797	Stage~2 uses MCC as the primary metric instead, for three reasons:
   798	(1)~the stability component of hotspot-score measures bootstrap reproducibility under position-level subsampling, but the subsampling behavior differs fundamentally across pathogens with different alignment lengths (340--1,330 AA) and MSA sizes (530--5,019 unique sequences), making cross-pathogen stability values non-comparable;
   799	(2)~MCC utilizes all four cells of the confusion matrix (TP, TN, FP, FN), providing a balanced evaluation under the extreme class imbalance inherent in hotspot detection (positive rates 0.7\%--15.9\% across the 11 pathogens);
   800	and (3)~separating the evaluation metric between stages allows Stage~1 to assess detection \textit{reliability} (via stability) and Stage~2 to assess detection \textit{accuracy} (via MCC), each optimized for its analytical purpose.
   801	MCC is formally defined as:
   802	\begin{equation}
   803	\text{MCC} = \frac{TP \times TN - FP \times FN}{\sqrt{(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}
   804	\label{eq:mcc}
   805	\end{equation}
   806	where $TP$, $TN$, $FP$, and $FN$ denote true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively.
   807	MCC ranges from $-1$ (complete disagreement) through $0$ (random prediction) to $+1$ (perfect prediction), and unlike F1, it utilizes all four cells of the confusion matrix, making it robust to class imbalance.
   808	When any factor in the denominator is zero (e.g., no positive predictions), MCC is conventionally defined as 0.
   809	MCC was selected as the primary metric because in hotspot detection, where positive positions (convergent evolution sites) constitute a minority of the genome, it provides a more balanced evaluation than F1 for imbalanced classification problems. Chicco and Jurman~\cite{chicco2020mcc} systematically demonstrated that MCC provides more informative evaluation than F1 and accuracy in imbalanced binary classification.
   810	The stability component used in Stage 1 is excluded from Stage 2 because it is an internal consistency metric independent of external ground truth, and cross-pathogen comparability of Bernoulli masking effects has not been validated given the wide variation in sequence length and MSA size across the 11 pathogens.
   811	
   812	\subsubsection{Three-way ANOVA ($\omega^2$)}
   813	\label{subsec:9pathogen_statistics}
   814	
   815	A three-way ANOVA is performed with scoring type (20 levels), detection family (14 levels), and pathogen (11 levels) as factors.
   816	The three-way ANOVA model includes all three main effects (scoring, family, pathogen) and all three two-way interactions (scoring $\times$ family, scoring $\times$ pathogen, family $\times$ pathogen). The three-way interaction was not estimated because the design uses one observation per (scoring, family, pathogen) cell once detector-variant scores within a family are aggregated to the family-level mean ($n_{\text{cell}} = 1$ at the family-level grid; $20 \times 14 \times 11 = 3{,}080$ cells), so the three-way term is non-identifiable without additional within-cell replication; a power analysis suitable for the $n = 11$ pathogen factor and a Bayesian partial-pooling alternative are flagged as future work in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
   817	Partial omega-squared ($\omega^2_p$) was computed as the bias-corrected estimate of variance explained. Type~II sum of squares was used because it does not depend on the order of factor entry and provides unbiased estimates when interactions are present. Under Cohen's benchmarks for behavioral sciences~\cite{cohen1988statistical}, $\omega^2 > 0.14$ indicates a large effect; however, these thresholds were developed for psychology experiments and may require calibration for computational benchmarks where effect sizes tend to be larger due to deterministic algorithm behavior. With $N = 8{,}580$, the central limit theorem ensures robustness to non-normality of MCC values.
   818	Levene's test indicated heterogeneous variances across groups ($p < 0.05$); however, with $N = 8{,}580$ observations and a balanced design, ANOVA is robust to moderate violations of homoscedasticity.
   819	As a safeguard, all ANOVA findings were confirmed by the nonparametric Kruskal--Wallis test, which makes no distributional assumptions.
   820	Specifically, the Kruskal--Wallis test applied to the scoring main effect yielded $H = 277.9$, $p < 10^{-47}$, consistent with the parametric ANOVA result; this concordance confirms that the ANOVA conclusions are not artifacts of distributional assumptions. An additional Aligned Rank Transform (ART) two-way ANOVA on the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction (Wobbrock et al.\ 2011 procedure) yielded a rank-scale interaction $\omega^2 = 0.277$ with $F_{190, 2860} = 7.33$ and $p = 8.6 \times 10^{-141}$, distribution-free confirmation that the interaction is large and significant.
   821	No family-wise multiple testing correction (e.g., Bonferroni, Holm) was applied to the ANOVA results because the analysis is exploratory rather than confirmatory: the goal is to decompose variance sources, not to test individual pairwise comparisons. The Friedman test and LOPO cross-validation provide independent confirmation without requiring correction. For the vaccine escape Fisher's exact tests (3 comparisons), significance at $p < 0.01$ (H3N2, HIV-1) exceeds the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of $\alpha/3 = 0.017$.
   822	Following Cohen's effect size benchmarks~\cite{cohen1988statistical}, $\omega^2$ values are interpreted as small (0.01), medium (0.06), and large ($\geq 0.14$):
   823	\begin{equation}
   824	\omega^2 = \frac{SS_{\text{effect}} - df_{\text{effect}} \times MS_{\text{error}}}{SS_{\text{total}} + MS_{\text{error}}}
   825	\label{eq:omega_squared}
   826	\end{equation}
   827	where $SS_{\text{effect}}$ is the sum of squares for the factor of interest, $df_{\text{effect}}$ its degrees of freedom, $MS_{\text{error}}$ the mean square of the residual error, and $SS_{\text{total}}$ the total sum of squares.
   828	The $\omega^2$ values of main effects and two-way interactions are compared to identify the primary sources of performance variation.
   829	
   830	\subsubsection{LOPO Cross-Validation (Leave-One-Pathogen-Out)}
   831	
   832	The best-performing combination (scoring $\times$ detection) is selected from $n-1$ of 11 pathogens, applied to the held-out pathogen, and generalization performance is evaluated.
   833	The best-performing combination is defined as the (scoring, family) pair with the highest mean MCC across the $n-1$ training pathogens.
   834	Through 11 iterations, the concordance rate between training-best and test-best (oracle) combinations and the performance gap are computed.
   835	Under random selection from 280 possible combinations ($20 \times 14$), the expected concordance rate is approximately 0.36\%.
   859	\label{subsec:weight_sensitivity_methods}
   860	To verify the robustness of assigning equal weights ($1/3$) to the three components of the hotspot-score, a generalized weighted hotspot-score is defined:
   861	\begin{equation}
   862	\text{hotspot-score}_w = w_r \cdot \text{recall} + w_p \cdot \text{precision} + w_s \cdot \text{stability}
   863	\label{eq:weighted_hotspot_score}
   864	\end{equation}
   865	where $w_r + w_p + w_s = 1$ and each weight lies in the range $[0.05, 0.95]$.
   866	Rankings of the five methods are computed across a total of 171 weight combinations to analyze the proportion of weight space in which MutClust-Hybrid maintains first place (rank robustness).
   867	Additionally, rankings are separately presented for seven application scenarios, including early warning (recall-emphasis), vaccine design (precision-emphasis), and monitoring (stability-emphasis).
   868	
   869	\textbf{Statistical Validation Methods.}
   870	\label{subsec:statistical_methods}
   871	The following three methods are applied to assess the statistical robustness of the benchmark results.
   872	
   873	\textit{Bootstrap confidence intervals}: Region-level bootstrap is performed using the seven functional regions as units.
   874	In each iteration, seven regions are sampled with replacement to construct a bootstrap ground truth, and the detection results from the full data are re-evaluated against this bootstrap ground truth.
   875	This design captures the uncertainty in ground truth definition---variation in evaluation depending on which functional regions are included---and avoids the effective size reduction bias that occurs with individual position resampling.
   876	
   877	\textit{Permutation test}: Two permutation approaches are employed.
   878	(1)~Random label shuffling: Through 1,000 random permutations of ground truth labels, it is tested whether the observed metrics significantly exceed random expectation.
   879	(2)~Circular permutation: The H-score vector is rotated by a random offset $k$ ($H_i \rightarrow H_{(i+k) \bmod N}$), hotspots are re-detected from the rotated scores, and evaluated against the original ground truth.
   880	This approach preserves the spatial autocorrelation structure (cluster pattern) of H-scores while randomizing only the relationship with genomic positions, generating a more conservative null distribution than random label shuffling.
   881	The p-value is calculated as $count / n_{\text{perm}}$ (the proportion of null distribution values that equal or exceed the observed value).
   882	
   883	\textit{Pairwise comparison}: A paired bootstrap design that evaluates two methods simultaneously on the same bootstrap resample, testing the statistical significance of hotspot-score differences between methods.
   884	
   885	\subsection{Stage~3: Multi-Source Information Integration Methods}
   886	\label{subsec:stage3_methods}
   887	
   888	Stage~3 layers an information-integration analysis on top of the Stage~2 evaluation matrix. The same 20 scoring types are decomposed into 10 underlying positional features (homoplasy, entropy, frequency, rare-variant frequency, dN/dS proxy, pLDDT, SASA, Grantham distance, ESM-2 LLR, semantic change), and three ablation analyses are performed on an EqualWeight ensemble of those 10 features:
   889	(i)~\emph{leave-one-feature-out}: each feature is removed in turn and the change in mean MCC ($\Delta$MCC) is reported;
   890	(ii)~\emph{group ablation}: features are partitioned into Frequency-only (3), Freq~+~Phylogeny (4), Freq~+~Structure (5), Freq~+~DL (5), and All-10, and group-wise mean MCC is compared;
   891	(iii)~\emph{cumulative addition}: features are added in descending order of single-feature AUC and the cumulative mean MCC is computed at $k = 1, 2, \ldots, 10$ to identify the minimum subset that recovers a target proportion of the All-10 performance.
   892	Per-pathogen feature AUC is computed via threshold sweeping (no model training), and a complementary multivariate Random Forest (\texttt{n\_estimators}~=~500, default scikit-learn hyperparameters, 5-fold cross-validation per pathogen) reports relative feature importances for triangulation.
   893	The Stage~3 evaluation set is the same 11 pathogens used in Stage~2, optionally extended to 12 pathogens by adding Zika (E protein, 505~AA) when the analysis benefits from increased per-feature statistical power; the 11-vs-12 distinction is reported transparently in every Stage~3 table caption (Section~\ref{subsec:feature_ablation}).
   894	A vaccine-escape cross-validation analysis is then performed on the 3 of 11 pathogens with curated antibody-escape annotations (H3N2, SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1; 2{,}340 enrichment evaluations) and audited for circularity against Layer~A (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation_escape}).

   553	In all 6 pathogens, the best scoring type differs between Layer~A and Layer~C (Table~\ref{tab:layer_a_vs_c}). The Spearman rank correlations between Layer~A and Layer~C scoring rankings are non-significant for 4 of 6 pathogens (SARS-CoV-2: $\rho = -0.13$; H3N2: $\rho = -0.11$; HIV-1: $\rho = 0.27$; EV-A71: $\rho = -0.18$), confirming that Layer~C provides an independent evaluation dimension. RSV ($\rho = 0.85$) and Rabies ($\rho = 0.86$) show strong positive correlations. \textbf{Post-hoc rationalisation check}: the 20 scoring formulas were defined prior to per-pathogen evaluation (Chapter~\ref{ch:mutbench}); the per-pathogen MCC ranking is deterministic given the design and the biological rationale per pathogen is interpretive only. The Layer~A vs.\ Layer~C divergence above provides an independent ranking that constrains the rationale --- a hypothetical third ground truth could shift winners again, but the *pathogen-adaptive heterogeneity itself* would only be reinforced (more ground truths $\Rightarrow$ more independent rankings $\Rightarrow$ stronger evidence that no single information source dominates).
   554	In practice, when Layer~A and Layer~C indicate different optimal scoring types, the choice depends on the research objective: Layer~A rankings should be prioritized for immune evasion surveillance, while Layer~C rankings are more appropriate for functional impact assessment such as DMS-guided drug target prioritization.

   608	The DMS-unavailable subgroup is \emph{not} systematically worse; if anything, its best-MCC mean is slightly higher, which argues against the hypothesis that Layer~A alone is a weaker ground truth than Layer~A+C. Two mechanisms likely explain the higher values in the DMS-unavailable group: (i)~HCV's Layer~A is defined by hypervariable-region boundaries rather than point positions, which inflates detectability; (ii)~Norovirus and Influenza~B have denser Layer~A sets, making true positives more abundant and MCC easier to attain. Conversely, the DMS-available group contains pathogens (RSV, Rabies, EV-A71) with narrow, sparse Layer~A sets that cap the achievable MCC.
   609	
   610	\textbf{Interpretation}: the main Stage~2 conclusions (scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction dominance, LOPO non-generalization, Friedman non-significance) are supported by both subgroups. The DMS-unavailable pathogens contribute informative signal despite lacking functional validation, and their inclusion does not bias the interaction finding in a direction favorable to the conclusion. However, a mechanistic interpretation of the best scoring type in the DMS-unavailable subgroup remains one step less grounded than in the DMS-available subgroup, since only the latter can be back-checked against independent experimental fitness data; the DMS-unavailable subgroup's results should be treated as phylogenetic-pattern evidence rather than functional-effect evidence.

Feature importances were extracted as mean decrease in impurity (Gini importance), and model performance was evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation AUC.\footnote{Caveat on CV design. The 5-fold split is at the position level within each pathogen, so adjacent residues with correlated features can land in different folds. This makes the reported AUC prone to spatial-autocorrelation leakage and should be interpreted as a feature-complementarity illustration rather than a generalisation estimate; a region-blocked or protein-domain-blocked CV is queued for future work.}
   686	
   687	Figure~\ref{fig:feature_importance_grid} presents the feature importance distributions across all 11 pathogens. Three patterns are notable.
   688	
   689	\textbf{First, the dominant feature differs across pathogens.}
   690	For SARS-CoV-2, ESM-2 LLR dominates (importance = 0.331), followed by pLDDT (0.286) and the newly added SASA (0.202)---all three are non-frequency features. For H3N2, pLDDT remains the most important feature (0.338), with semantic change (0.105) providing complementary information from the deep learning category. For Norovirus, homoplasy dominates (0.345), consistent with its near-perfect univariate AUC (0.944). For HIV-1, ESM-2 LLR (0.214) and homoplasy (0.143) share importance. For HCV, the dN/dS proxy (0.145), homoplasy (0.139), and Grantham distance (0.116) contribute complementary information in the multivariate context, despite the high univariate correlation between dN/dS proxy and frequency ($\rho = 0.87$).
   691	
   692	\textbf{Second, expanding from 6 to 10 features improves cross-validation AUC.}
   693	Norovirus achieves the highest cross-validation AUC (0.899). SARS-CoV-2 improves from 0.554 (6 features) to 0.606 (10 features), and MERS improves from 0.537 to 0.875, demonstrating that the additional features---particularly SASA and semantic change---capture information relevant to hotspot prediction that was previously missing. RSV improves to 0.737, HCV to 0.700, and the remaining pathogens achieve: H3N2 (0.791), HIV-1 (0.802), Dengue (0.782), Influenza~B (0.756).
   694	
   695	\textbf{Third, the importance rankings differ from univariate AUC rankings.}
   696	For HIV-1, entropy has the highest univariate AUC (0.730) but ranks third in Random Forest (RF) importance (0.127) behind ESM-2 LLR (0.214) and homoplasy (0.143), because entropy and frequency are highly correlated ($\rho = 0.97$, see Figure~\ref{fig:feature_correlation}) and share importance in the RF model while ESM-2 LLR provides non-redundant information. This demonstrates that multivariate analysis reveals complementary feature contributions that univariate analysis cannot capture.

   889	
   890	\textbf{Key findings:}
   891	All three pathogens achieve nominally significant vaccine escape enrichment ($p < 0.05$) with the optimal scoring--detection combination; after Bonferroni correction across 780 combinations, H3N2 and HIV-1 survive while SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory only. The best scoring \emph{category} for escape enrichment agrees with the Layer~A benchmark results at the category level (Phylogenetic for H3N2, Frequency for HIV-1), though the top scoring \emph{type} within that category can differ between the two evaluations (HIV-1 Layer~A best is \textit{entropy} with Wavelet(t{=}2.0), MCC 0.275; HIV-1 escape best is \textit{freq} with Wavelet(t{=}1.5), enrichment 7.19$\times$---both frequency-derived and correlated at $\rho \approx 0.97$, Section~\ref{sec:information_analysis}). The strength of this concordance as \emph{external} evidence is pathogen-dependent: HIV-1 provides the cleanest external validation (82\% of its escape set lies outside Layer~A; see circularity audit below), whereas for H3N2 the 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap means that the concordance is largely a self-consistency check rather than independent replication.
   892	
   893	For H3N2, FUBAR Bayes factor captures 9 of 29 antigenic drift sites with 9.36-fold enrichment; 8 of those 9 captured positions are already in Layer~A (the audit paragraph below quantifies the resulting novel-only enrichment of 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$, not significant). The multi-source EqualWeight integration achieves 4.012-fold enrichment ($p = 0.0023$), capturing positions in both antigenic site~A (position~137) and site~B (positions~155, 159, 160, 186, 188), while frequency alone misses the structurally constrained site~B positions.
   894	
   895	A limitation of this analysis is that vaccine escape validation was feasible for only 3 of 11 pathogens (H3N2, HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2). chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:19:First, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$ at 20-type granularity; 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]; $\omega^2 = 0.103$ at 6-category granularity as a collinearity-robust lower bound) was the largest identified source of variance among modeled terms in the factorial ANOVA, with within-cell residual ($\omega^2 \approx 0.39$) representing unmodeled variation including the three-way interaction (Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:stage2_anova}).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:71:Layer~C (DMS functional fitness) is based on published DMS datasets~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}, and for pathogens without available DMS data, functional fitness validation cannot be performed.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:129:(2)~indel and protein language model integration, developing gap-handling strategies for the H-score framework and incorporating ESM-2 log-likelihood ratios~\cite{lin2023esm2,meier2021language} or alternative protein language models such as ProtTrans~\cite{elnaggar2022prottrans} (and the multimodal ESM-3 generation, where benchmarking on viral proteins becomes available) as position-specific fitness scores;
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:139:The central result---that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 11-pathogen cluster-bootstrap 95\% interval [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest identified modeled variance component, alongside a within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$ that reflects further pathogen-level heterogeneity---empirically supports the algorithm selection principle~\cite{kerschke2019algorithm} and provides evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:157:Phylogenetic trees were inferred using IQ-TREE~2 with ModelFinder; selection pressure analysis used HyPhy~v2.5 (FUBAR, MEME); protein language model scores used the \texttt{esm2\_t33\_650M\_UR50D} checkpoint; and thermodynamic stability was predicted using FoldX~5.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:158:All stochastic processes (bootstrap resampling, subsampling) used a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:159:Pathogen sequence data were collected from NCBI GenBank, and SARS-CoV-2 DMS data were obtained from the original data provided by Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms, dadonaite2024nature}.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:13:\label{sec:bootstrap_interpretation}
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:15:The wide 95\% confidence intervals observed in region-level BCa bootstrap (e.g., MutClust-Hybrid [0.323, 0.635]) reflect region-dependent recall sensitivity in small samples ($n = 7$): resamples dominated by high-signal regions (RBD) inflate recall, while low-signal-only resamples deflate it.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:16:Nevertheless, pairwise bootstrap comparisons show that differences between methods are significant ($p < 0.001$), because paired evaluation on the same resample cancels region-combination variability.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:85:The ESM-2 cross-paradigm validation (Section~\ref{subsec:esm_validation}) reinforces this: ESM-LLR is the top-ranked feature for SARS-CoV-2 but substantially outperformed by homoplasy for Norovirus (AUC $= 0.763$ vs.\ $0.944$), confirming that no single scoring paradigm dominates.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:230:Retrieve $\geq$200 protein-coding sequences from NCBI GenBank or GISAID, ensuring temporal and geographic diversity. Construct a multiple sequence alignment using MAFFT~\cite{katoh2013mafft} (${\sim}$5 minutes for 1{,}000 sequences).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:233:Compute scoring features in order of increasing computational cost: (i)~frequency and Shannon entropy from the MSA (seconds); (ii)~homoplasy counts via Fitch parsimony on an inferred phylogenetic tree (2--5 minutes); (iii)~ESM-2 log-likelihood ratios, requiring a GPU (3--5 minutes per protein); (iv)~structural features such as surface accessibility and interface proximity, requiring an AlphaFold2~\cite{jumper2021alphafold} predicted structure or an experimental PDB entry when available. Steps (i)--(iii) are applicable to any pathogen with $\geq$200 sequences and require no specialized hardware beyond a single GPU for ESM-2 inference; step (iv) can be omitted when no structural model exists, with moderate impact on detection performance. When structural features are available, the 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures 98\% of full-ensemble performance; without pLDDT, the remaining 3 features (homoplasy, entropy, frequency) still provide the dominant scoring signals.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:289:\label{sec:esm2_leakage}
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:291:ESM-2~\cite{lin2023esm2} was trained on UniRef50/UniRef90, which contains viral protein sequences, and the 11 target proteins in our benchmark (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 Spike, HIV-1 gp120, H3N2 HA) are likely present in the training corpus.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:303:The three-way ANOVA treats pathogen as a fixed effect, which is appropriate for inference about these 11~specific pathogens but does not support generalization to all RNA viruses. A mixed-effects model treating pathogen as a random effect would enable broader inference; however, with only 11~pathogen-level observations, frequentist random-effect estimation is unreliable (Bolker et al.~\cite{bolker2009glmm} recommend $\geq$5--6 levels per random factor, ideally more). A natural alternative for the small-$n$ regime is \emph{Bayesian hierarchical (partial-pooling) modeling}, which we have additionally fit. With half-Cauchy priors on the between-scoring, between-pathogen, between-family, interaction-, and residual-scale parameters and a vague Normal prior on the grand mean, the NUTS posterior over the cell-level model (PyMC 5.28; 2~chains $\times$ 800 draws after 800 tuning steps; $\hat R \leq 1.01$ for all variance components) yields a posterior mean of $\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.252$ with 95\% HDI $[0.188, 0.314]$ and posterior probability $\Pr(\omega^2_{\text{int}} > 0.14) = 0.996$. The partial-pooling estimate sits slightly below the fixed-effect point (0.296) as expected from variance shrinkage, but the credible-interval lower bound (0.188) still essentially coincides with the cluster-bootstrap lower bound (0.195) and remains above Cohen's large-effect threshold ($\omega^2 > 0.14$) under both inferential frames. As the benchmark expands to 20--30+ pathogens, frequentist mixed-effects modeling additionally becomes feasible by the Bolker criterion.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:337:Despite the small sample size ($n=11$), the Friedman test yielded $p=0.990$, indicating that no single method can be reliably distinguished as superior across all pathogens. This is consistent with the LOPO finding (0/11 match rate) that each pathogen requires a unique best-performing combination. \textbf{Sampling-quality vs.\ pathogen-dependence}: the smallest-sample pathogens (Rabies $n_{\text{seq}} = 2{,}038$ but truncated 491 AA; EV-A71 $n_{\text{seq}} = 662$, 261 AA) do attain the lowest oracle MCCs (0.248, 0.260), so a sampling-quality confound is not zero. However, the technical-covariate sensitivity analysis (Section~\ref{sec:scoring_input_heterogeneity}, $\rho_L = -0.73$, $\rho_P = +0.64$) shows the joint covariate effect is subsumed by the pathogen main effect ($\omega^2 = 0.117$), and the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction (0.296) is a within-pathogen quantity that survives this absorption (see the ANCOVA bound there). Excluding the two smallest-sample pathogens (re-running the ANOVA on $n = 9$) shifts the headline interaction by less than the cluster-bootstrap CI half-width, so the pathogen-dependence finding is not a small-sample artifact of the two weakest panels.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:20:For RNA viruses, which exhibit mutation rates of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$ substitutions per nucleotide per replication cycle~\cite{holmes2009evolution}, the interplay between high mutation supply and strong selective pressure creates pronounced mutational clustering in functionally critical regions.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:44:Phylogeny-aware methods such as TreeTime~\cite{sagulenko2018treetime}, BEAST~\cite{suchard2018beast}, and HyPhy~\cite{kosakovsky2020hyphy} can address this but require high-quality phylogenetic trees and have limited reliability in densely sampled datasets~\cite{turakhia2020ultrafast}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:57:Rather than detecting spatial clusters of mutations, codon-based methods such as MEME (Mixed Effects Model of Evolution)~\cite{kosakovsky2020hyphy} and FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian AppRoximation)~\cite{kosakovsky2020hyphy} estimate the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rates ($\omega = dN/dS$) at each codon position.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:104:Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms} extended this to the full-length Spike protein by measuring pseudovirus cell entry fitness, identifying positions critical for viral entry beyond the RBD.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:105:Lee et al.~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms} performed DMS of influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA), demonstrating that DMS fitness measurements can predict the evolutionary fates of naturally circulating variants.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:132:\textbf{ESM-2}~\cite{lin2023esm2,rives2021biological} is a masked language model with 650 million parameters, trained on approximately 250 million protein sequences from the UniRef database.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:256:(1)~quantification of the scoring--pathogen interaction through three-way ANOVA, revealing that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 11-pathogen cluster-bootstrap 95\% interval [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest modeled variance component (within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$);
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:59:Detection methods were therefore evaluated against three complementary ground truths: \textbf{functional regions} (439 AA, 34.5\% of Spike; domain annotations including RBD, NTD supersite, furin cleavage, fusion peptide, HR1, HR2), \textbf{DMS-escape} (252 positions, 19.8\%; top 20th percentile of experimentally measured fitness effects~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}), and \textbf{convergent evolution} (97 positions, 7.6\%; literature-based recurrent positive selection sites~\cite{cao2023ba286,carabelli2023convergent}).

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:176:Region-level BCa bootstrap CIs~\cite{efron1987better} (1,000 resamplings, $n = 7$ Spike regions; hereafter \emph{region-level BCa CI}) gave a 95\% CI of [0.323, 0.635] for MutClust-Hybrid hotspot-score; pairwise bootstrap comparisons confirmed all score differences are significant ($p < 0.001$). Two additional BCa CIs reported later in this dissertation use different resampling units and should be interpreted separately: the \emph{combination-level BCa CI} [0.047, 0.202] for the best single scoring--detection combination's mean MCC (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_bootstrap}, 1{,}000 resamples over 11 pathogens) and the \emph{cluster bootstrap CI} [0.195, 0.333] for the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction $\omega^2$ (Section~\ref{subsec:anova_diagnostics}, 1{,}000 cluster resamples over 11 pathogens).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:247:Stage~2 uses MCC rather than hotspot-score because the stability component (Jaccard-based subsampling reproducibility) requires bootstrap validation that has not been cross-validated across all 11 pathogens with their widely varying alignment lengths (261--1,330 AA) and MSA sizes (530--5,019 unique sequences). MCC provides a single, well-established metric that is robust to class imbalance and does not require subsampling.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:329:Second, the best detection family also varies: KDE (4 pathogens), Wavelet (3), SlidingTest (1), Bayes (1), MutClust (1), and SWAN (1). The FUBAR spotlight analysis (Figure~\ref{fig:fubar_spotlight}) illustrates how phylogenetic scoring can outperform all other information types for specific pathogens such as H3N2.

Cohen tier per~\cite{cohen1988statistical}: small $\omega^2 \in [0.01, 0.06)$, medium $\in [0.06, 0.14)$, large $\geq 0.14$.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:390:\textbf{Key finding}: the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) is the largest modeled component, exceeding all main effects and other two-way interactions and qualifying as large under Cohen's $\omega^2 > 0.14$ threshold~\cite{cohen1988statistical}. The within-cell residual ($\omega^2 \approx 0.39$, absorbing the three-way interaction and parameter-variant noise) is comparable in magnitude, so ``largest source'' in this dissertation reads as ``largest modeled component.''
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:394:The same 8{,}580-evaluation dataset is re-examined under three statistical lenses: ANOVA (interaction $\omega^2 = 0.296$, 11-pathogen cluster-bootstrap 95\% interval [0.195, 0.333]); Friedman ($\chi^2 = 7.69$, $p = 0.990$); LOPO (0/11 matches, gap 0.265). The three lenses are consistency checks on the same data, not independent replications; an independent replication on a disjoint pathogen panel is deferred to future work.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:427:These results are consistent with a key interpretation: the 0/11 exact-match rate is itself not unexpected given 780 unique scoring--detection combinations (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}), so the primary evidence for pathogen-adaptive method selection is not the exact-match rate but the accompanying mean oracle-vs-generalized MCC gap of 0.265 (family-level oracle mean 0.297; generalized mean 0.032), which quantifies the performance cost of ignoring pathogen identity.\footnote{All LOPO arithmetic in this section uses the scoring~$\times$~detection-family aggregation (280 combinations); the larger detector-variant oracle of 0.341 reported in the per-combination headline (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_bootstrap}) corresponds to the finer scoring~$\times$~detector-variant grid (780 combinations) and is not directly comparable to the 0.265 gap.}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:449:\label{subsec:9pathogen_bootstrap}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:450:The best single combination across all pathogens was evaluated using BCa bootstrap.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:475:\label{subsec:esm_validation}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:476:To test whether the benchmark findings generalize beyond MSA-derived scoring formulas, an independent scoring paradigm was evaluated: the ESM-2 protein language model (650M parameters)~\cite{lin2023esm2}. ESM-2 computes per-position log-likelihood ratios (ESM-LLR) from a single consensus sequence using learned evolutionary representations, requiring no multiple sequence alignment. This provides orthogonal validation of the benchmark framework because the scoring signal originates from a fundamentally different methodology---a deep neural network trained on millions of protein families---rather than from the same MSA used by the other scoring formulas.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:488:The $\omega^2$ estimates should therefore be interpreted as indicative effect sizes rather than precise variance decompositions. The cluster bootstrap reported below is explicitly the effective-$N$-aware correction: resampling is performed \emph{at the pathogen level} (11 independent clusters) rather than at the evaluation level ($N = 8{,}580$), which naturally absorbs the within-pathogen dependence. Specifically, 1{,}000 cluster-bootstrap resamples over the 11 pathogens yield a 95\% CI of $[0.195, 0.333]$ for the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction; this CI width (0.138) already reflects the effective-$N$ contraction and does not require an additional $\sqrt{N/N_{\text{eff}}}$ correction.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:489:For sensitivity, a naive $N = 8{,}580$ bootstrap (ignoring pathogen-cluster structure) yields a narrower CI of $[0.260, 0.321]$; the wider cluster-bootstrap CI is the more honest reference for inference about the pathogen-dependence conclusion. The effect remains above Cohen's large-effect threshold ($\omega^2 > 0.14$) under both bootstrap schemes and at the more conservative 6-category aggregation. The 11-cluster regime is below the rule-of-thumb $\geq 30$ for percentile-bootstrap CI calibration; a wild-cluster bootstrap (Cameron, Gelbach \& Miller 2008) is the standard sharper alternative for $G \leq 30$ and is recommended for any future cycle that revises the headline interval. For the present cycle the percentile interval is reported with the explicit caveat that small-cluster coverage may be slightly anticonservative; the lower bound (0.195) sits well above Cohen's large threshold even under generous coverage adjustment.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:563:\item \textbf{Interaction dominance (modeled)}: Among the modeled factors, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest component, exceeding all main effects and other two-way interactions; a within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$ captures the unmodeled three-way interaction and parameter-variant noise. chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:631:\item \textbf{Deep learning-based} (2 features): \textit{esm2\_llr} (ESM-2 protein language model log-likelihood ratio~\cite{lin2023esm2,rives2021biological}, measuring how surprising a mutation is relative to learned evolutionary constraints from 250M protein sequences) and \textit{semantic change} (mean cosine distance between wild-type and mutant ESM-2 embeddings at each position~\cite{hie2021learning}, measuring how much a mutation alters the protein's functional context).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:632:\item \textbf{Structure-based} (2 features): \textit{plddt} (AlphaFold2/ESMFold predicted local distance difference test score~\cite{jumper2021alphafold}, indicating structural confidence and disorder propensity) and \textit{SASA} (relative solvent accessible surface area computed from ESMFold-predicted structures using the Shrake--Rupley algorithm~\cite{shrake1973environment}, measuring surface exposure).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:636:These 10 features were selected from a broader set of 22 candidate information types identified from the literature. Features excluded from the analysis include: weighted contact number (WCN, high correlation with SASA, $r > 0.7$), intrinsic disorder prediction (largely redundant with pLDDT $< 50$~\cite{wilson2022alphafold}), co-mutation/mutual information (pairwise rather than per-position feature, incompatible with the univariate per-position analysis framework; additionally $O(L^2)$ computational cost), codon usage bias (weak association with hotspot status), and epitope/glycosylation distance (not uniformly available across all 11 pathogens). The selection criteria were: (1)~independence from existing features, (2)~applicability to all 11 pathogens, and (3)~prior validation in the literature.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:131:FASTA sequences for each pathogen were collected from NCBI GenBank by querying each target protein name (e.g., ``SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein'') with filters for complete coding sequences, excluding partial sequences and laboratory-derived constructs. No date range restriction was applied; all available sequences as of December 2024 were downloaded. Sequences with $>$5\% ambiguous bases (N) were removed, and identical sequences were deduplicated (the ``Unique seq.'' column in Table~\ref{tab:pathogen_data} reflects post-deduplication counts). Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) was performed for each surface protein (SARS-CoV-2: Spike, H3N2: HA, HIV-1: Env gp120, etc.) using MAFFT v7.505~\cite{katoh2013mafft} with the \texttt{--auto} mode, followed by computation of per-position mutation frequency and entropy.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:132:The \texttt{--auto} mode automatically selects among FFT-NS-2, L-INS-i, and G-INS-i based on the number and length of input sequences~\cite{katoh2013mafft}.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:315:For six pathogens with available Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) experimental data---SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, and EV-A71---experimentally measured fitness effects are used as ground truth.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:319:The DMS phenotypes measured differ by pathogen: cell entry fitness for SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2024nature} and RSV~\cite{simonich2026rsvdms}, viral replicative fitness for H3N2~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms}, viral growth in cell culture for HIV-1~\cite{haddox2018hiv1dms}, G-protein-mediated cell entry for Rabies~\cite{aditham2025rabies}, and replicative fitness for EV-A71~\cite{bakhache2025eva71}. Table~\ref{tab:dms_preprocessing} summarises the per-pathogen DMS preprocessing conventions adopted in this benchmark; cell-line and replicate-aggregation choices follow the released-source defaults except where noted.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:387:\footnotesize Layer C (DMS) sources: SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}, H3N2~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms}, HIV-1~\cite{haddox2018hiv1dms}, RSV~\cite{simonich2026rsvdms}, Rabies~\cite{aditham2025rabies}, EV-A71~\cite{bakhache2025eva71}.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:426:The DMS fitness data are derived from the full-length Spike protein characterization experiment by Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms, dadonaite2024nature}.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:434:This provides an experimental ground truth independent of the detection methods under evaluation, thereby avoiding the circularity of using bootstrap p-values for validation.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:613:Phylogenetic trees were reconstructed using IQ-TREE 2 with automatic model selection (ModelFinder) and 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. Homoplasy counts were computed by Fitch parsimony on the resulting maximum-likelihood tree, counting the number of independent origins of each amino acid substitution at each position.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:616:The dN/dS proxy uses the Nei--Gojobori method, while the three FUBAR-based scores~\cite{murrell2013fubar} provide Bayesian estimates of site-specific selection from the HyPhy framework, each capturing a different aspect of the posterior distribution.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:626:ESM-2 scores were computed using the \texttt{esm2\_t33\_650M\_UR50D} checkpoint (33 layers, 650M parameters).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:798:(1)~the stability component of hotspot-score measures bootstrap reproducibility under position-level subsampling, but the subsampling behavior differs fundamentally across pathogens with different alignment lengths (340--1,330 AA) and MSA sizes (530--5,019 unique sequences), making cross-pathogen stability values non-comparable;
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:817:Partial omega-squared ($\omega^2_p$) was computed as the bias-corrected estimate of variance explained. Type~II sum of squares was used because it does not depend on the order of factor entry and provides unbiased estimates when interactions are present. Under Cohen's benchmarks for behavioral sciences~\cite{cohen1988statistical}, $\omega^2 > 0.14$ indicates a large effect; however, these thresholds were developed for psychology experiments and may require calibration for computational benchmarks where effect sizes tend to be larger due to deterministic algorithm behavior. With $N = 8{,}580$, the central limit theorem ensures robustness to non-normality of MCC values.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:822:Following Cohen's effect size benchmarks~\cite{cohen1988statistical}, $\omega^2$ values are interpreted as small (0.01), medium (0.06), and large ($\geq 0.14$):
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:845:Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) are computed for MCC values across 11 pathogens to quantify the performance variability of the best-performing combination across pathogens. With $n = 11$, the actual coverage of BCa intervals may be somewhat below the nominal 95\% level; these intervals should therefore be interpreted as approximate confidence intervals.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:873:\textit{Bootstrap confidence intervals}: Region-level bootstrap is performed using the seven functional regions as units.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:874:In each iteration, seven regions are sampled with replacement to construct a bootstrap ground truth, and the detection results from the full data are re-evaluated against this bootstrap ground truth.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:883:\textit{Pairwise comparison}: A paired bootstrap design that evaluates two methods simultaneously on the same bootstrap resample, testing the statistical significance of hotspot-score differences between methods.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:898:The full source code, configuration files, scoring scripts, detection-family implementations, ground-truth tables, statistical-analysis notebooks, and the 8{,}580-evaluation result archive are released under an open-source license (see Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}, Section~\ref{sec:code_availability} for the canonical repository URL, commit hash, and Zenodo DOI). The pinned random seed (\texttt{seed} = 42) governs all bootstrap, subsampling, and permutation analyses; library versions (Python~3.10, NumPy~1.24, SciPy~1.11, IQ-TREE~2, HyPhy~v2.5, ESM-2 \texttt{esm2\_t33\_650M\_UR50D}, FoldX~5) are pinned in the released environment file.

   131	\caption{Research overview. The study proceeds from identifying the information limitation (reliance on frequency/entropy) through systematic comparison of 10 information types via MutBench, to the key finding that the optimal information source differs by pathogen, culminating in external vaccine-escape validation on a Layer~A-disjoint subset (HIV-1, Bonferroni-significant) as the primary anchor for practical impact.}
   132	\label{fig:research_overview}
   133	\end{figure}
   134	
   135	
   136	\section{Research Contributions}
   137	\label{sec:intro_contributions}
   138	
   139	The research contributions of this study are as follows.
   140	
   141	\textbf{Contribution 1. MutBench: a systematic hotspot-detection benchmark across 11 RNA viruses.}
   142	MutBench is the broadest hotspot-detection benchmark to date, complementing concurrent fitness-regression benchmarks (ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}, ProteinGym v1.3~\cite{notin2025proteingym_v13}) by targeting region-level detection rather than per-variant fitness, and is designed to answer the question: \emph{which biological information source is most effective for which pathogen?}
   143	It organizes 10 information types into 20 scoring formulas across 6 categories (frequency, MSA-derived, phylogenetic, structural, AI-based, and composite), defines a three-layer ground truth framework (convergent evolution positives as Layer~A, purifying selection negatives as Layer~B, DMS experimental fitness as Layer~C), introduces the hotspot-score composite metric, and presents a two-stage experimental design combining in-depth SARS-CoV-2 analysis with a large-scale comparison across eleven pathogens.
   144	
   145	\textbf{Contribution 2. Statistical demonstration that the optimal biological information source differs fundamentally across pathogens ($\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.296$), with 9 distinct optimal information types across 11 pathogens and no cross-pathogen generalization (LOPO 0/11).}
   146	All eleven pathogens exhibited different best-performing combinations (LOPO cross-validation: 0/11 matches), with 9 distinct best-performing scoring types observed---including FUBAR phylogenetic selection scores for H3N2, protein language model scores for SARS-CoV-2 and RSV, and homoplasy for Norovirus.
   147	The Friedman test ($p = 0.990$) showed no reliably superior combination across all pathogens, consistent with pathogen-dependent optimality.
   148	The scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction is the largest modeled variance component ($\omega^2 = 0.296$, 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]; 6-category aggregation gives $\omega^2 = 0.103$ as a collinearity-robust lower bound). The conclusion rests on the interaction effect plus the vaccine-escape audit; LOPO 0/11 alone is null-consistent under permutation (Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:stage2_anova}).
   149	
   150	\textbf{Contribution 3 (two-part).} \textit{(3a) Multi-source integration infrastructure}: a compact 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) retains $\approx$98\% (97.6\%, 0.081/0.083 mean MCC) of the full 10-feature EqualWeight ensemble on the 12-pathogen Stage~3 panel under uniform-weight LOPO top-10\% evaluation (numerical equivalence, no paired-test significance), and the EqualWeight integration achieves a statistically significant 4.012-fold H3N2 enrichment ($p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches fail. \textit{(3b) Externally-valid vaccine-escape enrichment, anchored on HIV-1}: the Layer-A-disjoint subset of HIV-1 escape positions (37 of 45) yields a direct novel-only enrichment of $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ (worst-case Bonferroni-adjusted Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$); H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is a self-consistency check (69\% Layer~A overlap); SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory after multiple-comparison correction.
   151	A systematic analysis of 10 biological information types---spanning sequence statistics, phylogenetic signals, protein language models, structural properties, and chemical characteristics---reveals that the most discriminative single feature (per-feature AUC) differs across pathogens (e.g., homoplasy for Norovirus, pLDDT for H3N2, ESM-2 for SARS-CoV-2), complementing the Stage~2 MCC-optimal scoring results in Contribution~2.
   152	Feature ablation identifies a 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) that captures $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of integrated performance.
   153	Multi-source integration reduces the experimental search space for hotspot validation, achieving H3N2 vaccine escape enrichment of 4.012$\times$ ($p = 0.0023$), while pathogen-optimized scoring achieves up to 7.19$\times$ enrichment for HIV-1 on the Layer~A-disjoint (novel) portion of the escape set (Bonferroni-corrected $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); the headline H3N2 9.36$\times$ is dominated by Layer~A-overlap positions and, restricted to the 9 novel positions, drops to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant). The benchmark's external validation is therefore primarily carried by HIV-1, with H3N2/SARS-CoV-2 providing self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively (see Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} for the full circularity audit).
   154	
   155	These three contributions form a logical hierarchy: Contribution~1 provides the standardized evaluation infrastructure; Contribution~2 uses it to establish pathogen-dependent optimality; and Contribution~3 builds on this to demonstrate the practical value of pathogen-adaptive information selection.
   156	
   157	\section{Dissertation Organization}
   158	\label{sec:intro_organization}
   159	
   160	This dissertation comprises six chapters.
   161	
   162	\textbf{Chapter~\ref{ch:background}, Related Research} reviews the existing literature on viral mutation hotspot detection, benchmarking methodology, and the gap that motivated the development of MutBench.
   163

   193	\subsection{Cross-Validation via Vaccine Escape Enrichment}
   194	\label{sec:cross_validation_escape}
   195	
   196	A critical question for any benchmark is whether its rankings reflect genuine biological relevance or merely circular evaluation artifacts.
   197	The vaccine escape enrichment analysis across three pathogens (2{,}340 evaluations) provides \emph{partial} cross-validation of the Layer~A benchmark results, with the strength of external validation differing substantially by pathogen.
   198	
   199	\paragraph{Three-tier evidence rule.} Pathogens are assigned to one of three evidence tiers using two operational criteria evaluated jointly: (i)~\emph{Bonferroni survival} of the Fisher's exact $p$-value across 780 scoring--detection combinations ($p_{\text{adj}} < 0.05$), and (ii)~\emph{Layer~A independence}, defined as fewer than one-third of escape positions overlapping the pathogen's Layer~A set ($|\text{escape} \cap \text{Layer A}| / |\text{escape}| < 33\%$). A pathogen passing both criteria is classified as a \textbf{primary external anchor} (HIV-1: 18\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); a pathogen passing only (i)~is a \textbf{self-consistency check} (H3N2: 69\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$); a pathogen passing neither is reported as \textbf{exploratory} (SARS-CoV-2: $p_{\text{adj}} > 0.05$). The 33\% overlap threshold separates the three observed pathogens into distinct tiers without intermediate values; sensitivity to the threshold (25\%, 33\%, 50\%) does not change tier assignments for these three cases. With only three pathogens any threshold in $(18\%, 60\%)$ produces the same partition; the rule is therefore calibrated on observed data and explicitly underpowered as a *predictive* rule for new pathogens. Future cycles with additional escape-annotated pathogens will test whether the 33\% threshold remains the correct cut-point; the present work uses it as a transparent decision rule, not a generalised threshold.
   200	
   201	HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. A direct novel-only re-test on the 37 Layer~A-disjoint positions (best combination freq~$+$~Wavelet~$t = 1.5$) yields enrichment in the range $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ depending on how many of the 8 escape~$\cap$~Layer-A positions the detector also captures (sensitivity $k \in \{0, \ldots, 8\}$); even the conservative worst case ($k = 8$, all overlap positions detected) gives $7.16\times$ with Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$, which survives Bonferroni correction ($\times 780$) by more than nine orders of magnitude.
   202	In contrast, H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check: 20 of 29 escape positions (69\%) already lie in H3N2 Layer~A, so the high enrichment predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance. Restricting the calculation to the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions drops the enrichment to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant; Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} circularity audit).
   203	SARS-CoV-2's 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction and is reported as exploratory only.
   204	
   205	The benchmark is \emph{not a circular artifact} in the algorithmic sense (ground truth and scoring are computed independently), but the practical-value claim of Contribution~3 is carried primarily by HIV-1, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence.
   206	
   207	\textbf{Concurrent-benchmark task-orthogonality.} The MutBench panel overlaps with ViroGym (HIV, SARS-CoV-2, H3N2 are common) and EVEREST~v3 (HIV, SARS-CoV-2 forecasting clades), so a head-to-head leaderboard appears feasible in principle. We do not run one in this dissertation because the metric universes are structurally non-overlapping: ViroGym and EVEREST optimise per-variant fitness Spearman against DMS, while MutBench optimises per-region binary MCC against the 3-layer ground truth; converting between the two requires either (a) thresholding fitness predictions at a top-$k$ cutoff to obtain a binary region call (which throws away the continuous information ViroGym/EVEREST were optimised for), or (b) summarising MutBench detections into a fitness ranking (which throws away the spatial-clustering information MutBench was optimised for). Either reduction biases the comparison toward the receiving format. The principled task-aligned subset evaluation (binarise fitness predictions at top-$k$ thresholds matched to MutBench's positive-rate per pathogen, then compare MCC on the shared HIV/SARS-CoV-2/H3N2 panel) is queued as a defense-week sprint item (Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion} Table~\ref{tab:limitations_summary}); the present cycle's contribution is the *structural orthogonality argument* itself, which removes the head-to-head as a knock-down objection.
   208	
   209	This cross-validation is particularly important for the five pathogens without DMS data (Layer~C), where benchmark validity rests primarily on Layer~A.
   210	The EVEREST study and its v3 expansion~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} demonstrate that even with 45 DMS datasets, current models fail to reliably predict mutations in over half of the 40 WHO priority RNA viruses, with reliability worst for surface glycoproteins---an external finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in Chapter~\ref{ch:results}. For H3N2 specifically, the antigenic-cartography lineage of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic} and the recent PLM-based extensions of PLANT~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} target a prediction task complementary to MutBench's region-level detection; the 69\% Layer~A overlap reported above should therefore be interpreted as task-internal self-consistency rather than as a head-to-head antigenic-prediction claim.
   211	MutBench's combination of Layer~A benchmark rankings with independent vaccine escape validation provides complementary evidence that circumvents DMS data availability constraints, supporting the validity of Layer~A as a ground truth even for pathogens where DMS data are unavailable.

   214	\subsection{Practical Considerations for Public Health Surveillance}
   215	\label{sec:practical_surveillance}
   216	
   217	Given SARS-CoV-2's generation time ({$\sim$}5 days) and sequence submission delay ({$\sim$}14 days), a minimum 4-week window is required for real-time TC-freq alerts. A fundamental methodological limitation affecting all frequency-based approaches is phylogenetic non-independence.
   218	
   219	For public health practitioners, MutBench results can be operationalized through the following workflow when a novel pathogen or variant emerges: (1)~compute the 20 scoring types from the available MSA (requiring only sequence data and publicly available tools: MAFFT for alignment, HyPhy for FUBAR, ESM-2 for PLM scores, AlphaFold2 for structural features); (2)~if the pathogen belongs to a family already represented in MutBench (e.g., Coronaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Flaviviridae), use the family-level scoring recommendation from Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} as a starting point; (3)~if the pathogen is novel, apply the EqualWeight ensemble as a conservative baseline, which achieves 98\% of full-feature performance with only 4 core features (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency). This workflow integrates with existing surveillance platforms such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} and GISAID~\cite{shu2017gisaid}, which already provide the MSA inputs required by MutBench.
   220	
   221	\paragraph{Optimality ceiling vs robust default floor.} Contributions~2 and 3a are complementary rather than contradictory along a single axis. Contribution~2 characterises the \emph{ceiling}: when the pathogen is known and an MCC-optimal scoring type can be chosen, pathogen-specific selection is the mechanism that yields the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction and the 0.265 oracle-vs-generalised MCC gap. Contribution~3a characterises the \emph{floor}: when the pathogen is novel or labelled data are unavailable and a single default must be deployed across the panel, a uniform-weight 4-feature core recovers $\approx$98\% of the full 10-feature ensemble's mean MCC. The two claims are separated by what the operator knows: selection-aware deployment follows Contribution~2, while selection-unaware deployment follows Contribution~3a. The narrative has therefore been kept dichotomous throughout this thesis---specialised ceiling for informed use, generic floor for cold-start use---rather than being presented as a single ``best method'' recommendation.
